 Live .  1,136 viewing 1136 viewing Live page Updated 2 minutes ago First Eurovision Asia under way as world's biggest song contest heads to Bangkok
 Summary
 The first ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia is under way
 Eleven acts from the continent are taking to the stage in Bangkok, Thailand, vying to win the inaugural prize - here's tonight's running order 
 On stage there's a performance from a beatboxing collective, a number of ballads and a pop song called BAE - meet the finalists 
 Voting is already open, here's how you can cast yours 
 Eurovision Asia has been talked about for two decades, but never materialised - until now, our correspondent in Bangkok writes 
 Close form Who do you want to win?
 Get in touch Live Reporting
 Edited by Matt Spivey, with Jonathan Head reporting from the One Bangkok Forum
 Beatboxing Bangladeshi group up now published at 14:24 GMT 14:24 GMT 
 Image source, Ralph Larmann/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Beatmosphere laying down their vocals at the rehearsals
 Beatboxing and a cappella, you say? Why not. It is Eurovision after all. 
 Beatmosphere are a collective who originally formed and bring something different to tonight's other acts - no backing track. 
 Tumi Ele, which they're performing, is a masterclass in how a blend of human voices - using harmonies and replicating the sound of drums and basslines - can produce everything needed for a fully-rounded song.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Many of the contestants are showbiz veterans published at 14:23 GMT 14:23 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 Many of these contestants are experienced performers. Toc Tien from Vietnam has been in the business for 30 years, since she was a child. In Vietnam, she’s a mega celebrity. 
 Aina Abdul from Malaysia is also a huge star at home.
 When she was a child, Carmelle from the Philippines performed on the The Voice Kids. Since then, she's won talent competition show Tawag ng Tanghalan and even appeared on Pinoy Big Brother.
 As a reminder, the vote is now open - here's a reminder of how to cast yours. 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Eurovision winner Dara graces the stage, as game show begins... published at 14:21 GMT 14:21 GMT 
 Bulgarian pop star Dara - the champion of this year's Eurovision - is now on stage. 
 She's going to give us an extra-special version of Bangaranga", her winning song, during the grand final. 
 We're then shown a look ahead to Bulgaria's 2027 Eurovision Song Contest - as three fans are given the chance to win tickets to see the final. 
 Suddenly, Eurovision Song Contest Asia has turned into a game show...
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 This song is a female empowerment anthem, says Sobra-Sobra writer published at 14:15 GMT 14:15 GMT 
 Matt and Nika, who wrote and produced the Philippines entry Sobra-Sobra, tell the BBC that they're "very excited and nervous" about the performance.
 "We can't believe it's happening right now," Matt says.
 The song is a women's empowerment anthem, Nika explains. "The song really says you can be whoever you want to be," she says. 
 They add they're "lucky" that Carmelle will be performing the song. 
 "She's so professional," Matt says, while Nika adds that she "embodies" the song. 
 Filipinos love music, they both say, so they're confident that Eurovision could be a big success there.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Has Philippines' Carmelle 'figured it out'? published at 14:14 GMT 14:14 GMT 
 Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Carmelle in rehearsals for her performance
 An anthem of owning your own femininity is up next in the form of a pop ballad, with an impressive rap section.
 It's Carmelle - who has appeared in Pinoy Big Brother and was runner-up on The Voice Kids - representing the Philippines. 
 Her official biography on the Eurovision Asia website says her music career has "skyrocketed to new heights in recent years".
 In her song Sobra-Sobra, she says "I have figured it out" - but let's see if she's worked out how to win the competition.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Can Bhutan's bilingual vocalist clinch a win? published at 14:09 GMT 14:09 GMT 
 Image source, Ralph Larmann/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Nyendra performing at this year's rehearsals
 Bhutan's song Lhayi Semo - from folk-pop star Nyendra - was the first song to be announced for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia.
 The 24-year-old artist, who holds university degree in journalism and writes and produces his own songs, beat four other artists in a national competition to represent Bhutan. 
 Nyendra's music spans several genres - and languages, he performs his songs in both English and Dzongkha. 
 Let's see how his performance goes.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 This performance is a world away from Beck's government job published at 14:05 GMT 14:05 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 Beck's song for Mongolia has changed dramatically through rehearsals this week.
 The artist himself has an unusual background - a financier and economic adviser to the Mongolian government.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 A model, the Moon and a mood-shift: It must be Mongolia's turn published at 14:02 GMT 14:02 GMT 
 Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Beck performing at the rehearsals
 A full moon above the ocean is the backdrop to Mongolian crooner Beck's performance.
 He's next up to the stage, and his heartfelt performance of Chamguigeer (Without You) will be a change of pace from the performance we just saw from Laos.
 The Mongolian singer, actor, TV host and model, began his music career in the early 2000s as a member of the band Funk Beats, before going on the pursue his solo career.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Arena far from full for the first Eurovision Asia contest published at 14:02 GMT 14:02 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 The contestants are certainly putting on a show - but the One Bangkok Forum arena is not full. There's lots of space for us in the audience to move around. 
 Although this is the first event of its kind, publicity for Eurovision Asia has had limited impact here in Thailand. 
 People have travelled here from across the world for this, but not in large numbers.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Up next, BAE published at 13:57 GMT 13:57 GMT 
 Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Thinla at rehearsals for this year's final
 Thinla entered the music scene in Laos in 2021, and is now representing her country at Eurovision Asia.
 BAE has the vibe of an old-school, feel-good bop - it's a real crowd pleaser.
 Thinla is wearing a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit for her performance.
 Thinla completed her first tour of the US this year - how will she handle another international stage tonight?
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Cambodia's Monterey needs only a single spotlight for his performance published at 13:56 GMT 13:56 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 Monterey from Cambodia is now up, with his ballad Let It Go. 
 He’s on his own - no dancers, a single spotlight on his gold jacket and isolated against a black background.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Vietnam's Tóc Tiên opened contest with impressive choreography published at 13:53 GMT 13:53 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 The first act, Tóc Tiên from Vietnam, took to the stage in an elaborate fairy-like costume. 
 The choreography was impressive - hours of rehearsal clearly paid off.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'He learnt music by himself,' says family of Monterey published at 13:49 GMT 13:49 GMT 
 The family of Cambodian contestant Monetrey - who is on stage now - spoke to the BBC ahead of the show.
 His sisters say he's the youngest of six children and a self-taught musician.
 "He grew by himself, he learnt music by himself, and now he's here - it's just amazing," his sister says.
 The family travelled from France to watch him take the stage. They joke that he's already won - and quickly add: "but don't forget to vote Cambodia!"
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 A ballad? At Eurovision? Yes please, Cambodia published at 13:48 GMT 13:48 GMT 
 Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Monetrey at the rehearsals
 Next up is Cambodia's stripped-back ballad I Let You Go, written and performed by Monetrey.
 The young artist was the winner of Cambodia's selection show Cambodia's Finest Voice, where he beat six other artists for the spot. 
 Eurovision describes him as having a "strong visual universe and storytelling-driven approach" - let's see if he can get that across in his three-minute set on stage tonight. 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Vietnam's Tóc Tiên first to take to the stage published at 13:44 GMT 13:44 GMT 
 Image source, Eurovision Song Contest Asia/COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU Image caption, Tóc Tiên in full glam at the rehearsals
 Here we go!
 To kick off the first ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia, it's Vietnam's Tóc Tiên.
 Having been an entertainer for the past two decades, Tiên's career includes being a successful solo artist, a film and TV actress and hosting some of the country's biggest reality television shows.
 The song chosen by Tiên - EM TIÊN - was the winner of TV show The Sound of Vietnam, which saw five songs go head-to-head for the chance to represent the country.

 Before we begin - here's the running order published at 13:44 GMT 13:44 GMT 
 It's almost time for the first ever contestant in Eurovision Asia to take to the stage. 
 As Vietnam's Tóc Tiên gears up - here's the running order:
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Voting is open - how does it work? published at 13:41 GMT 13:41 GMT 
 The hosts have just explained that voting has already opened!
 A split-vote between the public and a jury of peers is synonymous with the Eurovision Song Contest.
 How will it work in this version of the contest? 
 Much the same. The public vote will be responsible for 50% of the result, with the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries of the participating countries.
 Then, a vote count from the rest of the world, translated into a certain number of points, will be awarded to each country.
 Oh yes, did we mention you can vote from anywhere in the world? Just access the vote on the website , external .
 Each person gets eight votes free - but the rules stipulate you must distribute your points among a minimum of three songs. 
 You can purchase ten extra votes.
 Viewers cannot vote for their own country - as is the case in the Eurovision Song Contest.
 Get ready to make your decision and have your say on who you think should win.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 First up, a quick round of introductions published at 13:38 GMT 13:38 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 The hosts of this final Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop have just appeared on stage.
 They're now introducing the 11 contestants from each of the participating countries.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 The atmosphere is building published at 13:36 GMT 13:36 GMT 
 Jonathan Head 
South East Asia correspondent, at the One Bangkok Forum 
 Image source, COURTESY OF VOXOVATION AND EBU The crowd is building itself up for the start of the Eurovision grand final. 
 The stage looks spectacular.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 The first ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia is under way in Bangkok published at 13:31 GMT 13:31 GMT Breaking 
 After a one minute countdown, Eurovision Asia is officially under way for the first time ever. 
 Eleven performers are set to dazzle the stage and represent their countries in this inaugural song contest. 
 It's been talked about for two decades but now it's actually happening - we'll be watching closely as the first ever winner of Eurovision Asia is announced.
 We'll bring you live text updates from the event - stay with us.
